lessons.title: journald and journalctl
lessons.goal:
Learn where Linux logs go on a systemd machine, how to write your own entries, and how to filter them by time, unit and priority.

Why it matters: the first step of almost every troubleshooting session is "what does the log say?". `journalctl` is the fastest way to ask precisely.

setup.note: Steps with sudo add and remove a small rsyslog rule. Journal output is shown as plain messages (`-o cat`), because the default format includes the host name.
commands: sudo rm -f /etc/rsyslog.d/90-lab.conf /var/log/lab.log; sudo systemctl try-restart rsyslog 2>/dev/null; true

steps.title: One place for logs
steps.text: `systemd-journald` collects messages from services (their stdout and stderr), the kernel, the syslog socket and audit. It stores them in a binary database with **fields** (unit, PID, priority, time), so you can query instead of grepping.

run.cmd: journalctl --disk-usage | sed -E 's/.*take up/Journals use/; s/ in the file system.*//'

steps.title: Write a log entry yourself
steps.text: `logger` sends a message to the journal. `-t` sets the tag (the program name) and `-p` the priority. Then `journalctl -t TAG` reads it back; `-o cat` prints only the message.

steps.title: Priorities
steps.text: Messages have one of 8 levels: 0 emerg, 1 alert, 2 crit, 3 err, 4 warning, 5 notice, 6 info, 7 debug. `-p err` shows **err and everything more severe**.

run.output:
an error to the lab file
something failed

hello from the lesson
something failed
all fine

steps.after: The first listing shows only the error. The second, with `-p info`, includes info and everything above it.

steps.title: The fields behind a message
steps.text: Every entry is a set of fields. `-o json` shows them all. We pick three with `jq`.

run.cmd: journalctl -t lab -n 1 -o json --no-pager | jq -r 'keys | map(select(startswith("_"))) | length | "\(.) trusted fields added by journald"'

steps.under: Fields that start with an underscore (`_PID`, `_UID`, `_SYSTEMD_UNIT`, `_COMM`) are added by journald itself and cannot be forged by the sender, which makes them reliable for audit questions such as "which unit logged this?".

steps.title: Filter by time, unit and field
steps.text: `--since` and `--until` take times such as `-5min` or `yesterday`. `-u` selects a unit. Any field can be used as `FIELD=value`.

steps.title: Follow new messages
steps.text: `journalctl -f` prints new messages as they arrive, like `tail -f`. Here we send one message after one second and stop after three seconds.

run.cmd: (sleep 1; logger -t lab 'live message') & timeout 3 journalctl -f -n 0 -t lab -o cat --no-pager; true

steps.title: Persistent or volatile?
steps.text: If `/var/log/journal` exists, logs survive a reboot. Otherwise they live in `/run/log/journal` (RAM) and are lost. Settings are in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`: `Storage=persistent`, `SystemMaxUse=`, `MaxRetentionSec=`.

run.cmd: [ -d /var/log/journal ] && echo 'persistent: logs survive a reboot' || echo 'volatile: logs are lost at reboot'
run.output: volatile: logs are lost at reboot

run.cmd: journalctl --list-boots --no-pager | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "boot(s) in the journal"}'

quiz.q: Which command shows messages of the unit `sshd` from the current boot?
quiz.explain: `-u` selects the unit and `-b` the boot.
The level and everything with a lower number.

options: journald adds them, the sender cannot forge them
quiz.explain: Fields starting with an underscore are trusted.

quiz.q: How do you keep logs across reboots?

check.scenario: A service crashed at 03:12 last night. Give the one command that shows what it logged in the ten minutes around it.
check.answer: `journalctl -u SERVICE --since '03:05' --until '03:15' --no-pager` (add `-p warning` to cut noise, `-k` for kernel messages such as an OOM kill at the same time: `journalctl -k --since '03:05' --until '03:15'`).

lessons.title: rsyslog, facilities and priorities
lessons.goal:
Learn the classic syslog model, add a rule that routes one facility to its own file, and see how it relates to the journal.

Why it matters: many tools (and many log-shipping setups) still speak syslog, and `/var/log/messages` and `/var/log/secure` on Red Hat systems are written by rsyslog.

setup.note: Steps with sudo add and remove a small rsyslog rule. Journal output is shown as plain messages (`-o cat`), because the default format includes the host name.
commands: sudo rm -f /etc/rsyslog.d/90-lab.conf /var/log/lab.log; sudo systemctl try-restart rsyslog 2>/dev/null; true

steps.title: Facility and priority
steps.text: Classic syslog classifies each message by **facility** (the kind of source: `auth`, `cron`, `daemon`, `kern`, `mail`, `user`, `local0` to `local7`) and **priority** (the same 8 levels as the journal). A rule is `facility.priority  destination`.

run.output:
*.info;mail.none;authpriv.none;cron.none action(type="omfile" file="/var/log/messages")
authpriv.* action(type="omfile" file="/var/log/secure")
mail.* action(type="omfile" file="/var/log/maillog" sync="on")
cron.* action(type="omfile" file="/var/log/cron")

steps.title: How logs reach rsyslog here
steps.text: On a systemd machine journald receives everything first, and rsyslog reads from it (`imjournal`), then writes the classic files.

run.output: load="imjournal" load="imklog" load="immark" load="imtcp" load="imudp" load="imuxsock"

steps.title: Add a rule
steps.text: We route facility `local3` (free for your own applications) to `/var/log/lab.log`, and restart rsyslog to load it.

run.output: rsyslogd: End of config validation run. Bye.

run.cmd: sudo systemctl restart rsyslog; echo restarted

steps.title: Send a message and find it
steps.text: `logger -p local3.info` sends to that facility. The file gets a classic line: time, host, tag and message. We cut the host name from the display.

run.cmd: logger -p local3.info -t lab 'to the lab file'; logger -p local3.err -t lab 'an error to the lab file'; sleep 1

run.output:
lab[3475484]: to the lab file
lab[3475485]: an error to the lab file

steps.under: rsyslog is a pipeline of **inputs** (journal, socket, files, network), **rules** (selectors and filters, also property-based: `if $programname == 'lab' then ...`) and **outputs** (files, remote hosts over TCP with TLS, databases, Elasticsearch). Remote forwarding is written `*.* @@loghost:514`.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Remove the rule and the file.

run.cmd: sudo rm /etc/rsyslog.d/90-lab.conf /var/log/lab.log; sudo systemctl restart rsyslog; ls /var/log/lab.log 2>&1 | sed 's/.*: //'

quiz.q: Where does rsyslog read from on a systemd system by default?
Which file typically holds general system messages on Oracle Linux?

options: Forwards all messages to loghost over TCP

check.scenario: Security wants all authentication logs shipped to a central server. Outline the rsyslog configuration and a reliability concern.
check.answer: A rule such as `authpriv.* action(type="omfwd" target="loghost" port="6514" protocol="tcp" StreamDriver="gtls" StreamDriverMode="1")` (TLS), with an action queue (`queue.type="LinkedList" queue.filename="fwd" queue.saveOnShutdown="on" action.resumeRetryCount="-1"`) so messages are buffered on disk when the server is unreachable. UDP loses messages silently.

lessons.title: logrotate: keeping logs from filling the disk
lessons.goal:
Learn how `logrotate` renames, compresses and removes old log files, write a configuration, test it safely, and understand `copytruncate`.

Why it matters: an unrotated log eventually fills the disk. A badly configured rotation breaks the application that is writing the log.

setup.note: Steps with sudo add and remove a small rsyslog rule. Journal output is shown as plain messages (`-o cat`), because the default format includes the host name.
commands: sudo rm -f /etc/rsyslog.d/90-lab.conf /var/log/lab.log; sudo systemctl try-restart rsyslog 2>/dev/null; true

steps.title: A log file to rotate
steps.text: We create a log of 200 lines (about 1.3 KB).

run.cmd: for i in $(seq 1 200); do echo "line $i of the log"; done > app.log; wc -c < app.log

steps.title: The configuration
steps.text: The file names the log and the rules: `rotate 3` keep three old copies, `size 1k` only rotate when bigger than 1 KB, `compress` gzip old copies, `missingok` no error if the file is absent, `notifempty` skip an empty file, `copytruncate` copy then truncate in place.

code.src:
/tmp/lab/app.log {
    rotate 3
    size 1k
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    copytruncate
}

run.output:
/tmp/lab/app.log {
    rotate 3
    size 1k
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    copytruncate
}

steps.title: Test with debug mode
steps.text: `-d` (debug) prints what **would** happen and changes nothing. Always test a new configuration this way first. `-s` sets the state file that remembers when each log was last rotated.

run.cmd: logrotate -d -s /tmp/lab/state app.logrotate 2>&1 | grep -E 'considering log|log needs rotating|rotating log|compressing'
run.output:
considering log /tmp/lab/app.log
  log needs rotating
rotating log /tmp/lab/app.log, log->rotateCount is 3
compressing log with: /bin/gzip

steps.title: Rotate for real
steps.text: `-f` forces a rotation. The log becomes `app.log.1.gz` (compressed) and `app.log` is empty again.

run.cmd: logrotate -f -s /tmp/lab/state app.logrotate; ls app.log* | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: Rotate again: numbers shift
steps.text: Each rotation moves `.1` to `.2`, `.2` to `.3`. With `rotate 3` the oldest copy is deleted. We add a log and rotate twice more.

run.cmd: for r in 1 2 3; do for i in $(seq 1 100); do echo "run $r line $i padding padding"; done > app.log; logrotate -f -s /tmp/lab/state app.logrotate; done; ls app.log* | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: copytruncate versus signals
steps.text: An application that keeps its log file **open** continues writing to the renamed file after a normal rotation (it holds the old inode). There are two fixes: tell it to reopen (a `postrotate` script that sends a signal or reloads the service) or use `copytruncate`, which copies the content and empties the original in place. `copytruncate` can lose lines written between the copy and the truncate.

run.cmd: systemctl is-enabled logrotate.timer 2>&1; grep -E '^(weekly|rotate|compress|dateext)' /etc/logrotate.conf | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.under: logrotate is not a daemon. It is started once a day by a systemd timer (or `/etc/cron.daily/logrotate`) and reads `/etc/logrotate.conf` plus `/etc/logrotate.d/*`. Each package ships its own file there.

options: Shows what would be done without changing anything

quiz.q: Why can a rotated log keep growing under the old name?
options: The application still has the old file open
quiz.explain: It holds the old inode open.

options: Lines written during the copy can be lost
quiz.explain: Copy and truncate are not atomic.

quiz.q: With `rotate 3`, how many old copies are kept?

check.scenario: After you configured rotation for an application, the log stays empty and the new lines vanish. Why, and how do you fix it?
check.answer: The application wrote to the renamed file via its open file descriptor (or it recreated nothing). Fix: add a `postrotate` that makes it reopen (`systemctl reload app` or the app's signal, often SIGHUP/USR1), or use `copytruncate`. Check with `lsof +L1` or `ls -l /proc/PID/fd`.

interview.q: What does journald store that plain text logs do not?
interview.a: Structured fields per entry (unit, PID, UID, priority, timestamps), indexed so you can filter reliably. See [the lesson](#/lesson/26/journald-journalctl).

interview.q: How do you see only errors of one service from last night?
What is the relationship between journald and rsyslog?
interview.a: journald collects first; rsyslog can read from it (imjournal) and write the classic /var/log files or forward them. See [rsyslog](#/lesson/26/rsyslog-facilities).
Facility: the source category (auth, cron, kern, local0-7). Priority: severity 0-7 (emerg to debug). A rule selects with `facility.priority`.

interview.q: How do you rotate a log that an application holds open?
interview.a: Use a postrotate that makes the app reopen it, or `copytruncate`. See [logrotate](#/lesson/26/logrotate).

interview.q: How do you make the journal persistent?
interview.a: Create `/var/log/journal` (or `Storage=persistent` in journald.conf) and restart journald; limit with `SystemMaxUse=`.

glossary.def: systemd's logging daemon that stores structured log entries.
The category of a log source, such as auth, cron or local3.
A syslog daemon that filters and routes log messages to files or remote hosts.
A tool run daily that rotates, compresses and removes old log files.
A logrotate option: copy the log then truncate the original in place.

commands.desc: Show a unit's messages since boot.
Write a message to the log.
Show space used by the journal.
